books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

primary_sources: United States v. E. C. Knight Co., 156 U.S. 1 (1895)

stimulus.text:
Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act (July 2, 1890):

“Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is hereby declared to be illegal.”

Five years later, the Supreme Court decided United States v. E. C. Knight Company (1895). The American Sugar Refining Company had bought four Philadelphia refineries and gained control of about 98 percent of sugar manufacturing in the United States. The Court ruled 8–1 against the government, holding that manufacturing was a local activity, not interstate commerce. Chief Justice Fuller wrote, “Commerce succeeds to manufacture, and is not a part of it.” In the same year, the Supreme Court upheld the use of the Sherman Act against Eugene V. Debs and the leaders of the Pullman strike, on the ground that the strike restrained interstate commerce.
stimulus.source_note: Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 1, July 2, 1890 (Statutes at Large, 26 Stat. 209); United States v. E. C. Knight Co., 156 U.S. 1 (1895), 8-1, Chief Justice Fuller; In re Debs, 158 U.S. 564 (1895). The 98 percent figure follows the Supreme Court Historical Society account of the case.

stem: The Sherman Act was aimed at business trusts, yet in 1895 the Court upheld its use against the leaders of the Pullman strike. What does that contrast best show?

options.text: A law aimed at trusts could strike workers while sparing the trusts
The Sherman Act was never used in any court at all
options.misconception: The Act was used in court in both the Knight case and the Debs case.

options.text: The Pullman strike was led by the sugar refiners of Philadelphia
options.misconception: The Pullman strike was a railroad strike led by Eugene V. Debs, not by sugar refiners.

options.text: The Sherman Act broke up the Sugar Trust in 1895
options.misconception: The Court ruled for the Sugar Trust, so no breakup followed.

rationales.A: The trust escaped because making sugar was local, while the strike was held to restrain interstate commerce.
rationales.B: The Act reached the courts in both cases, so it was used.
rationales.C: Debs led railroad workers in the Pullman strike, not sugar refiners.
rationales.D: The Court ruled for the Sugar Trust, so no breakup followed.
rationales.general:
Compare the two uses of one law.
1. The Sugar Trust kept its monopoly because manufacturing was called a local activity.
2. The Pullman strikers were stopped because their strike was said to restrain interstate commerce.
3. The same law that spared a sugar monopoly struck at organized workers.
4. Critics saw the contrast as proof that the law worked against labor, not against trusts.
Remember: one law can bite in two directions, so ask who felt it.
